 LITTLE ROCK, Ark. (KATV) — That “extra hour” you get when clocks fall back can feel like a little gift, until the next morning, when your body decides it didn’t get the memo.
 Sleep specialist Dr. Erin Creighton said the end of daylight saving time can throw people off because the clock changes overnight, but your internal body clock doesn’t adjust nearly as fast. Even though the fall-back switch sounds like it should mean more rest, it doesn’t always work out that way.
 Creighton explained that if someone normally wakes up at 6 a.m., their body may still pop awake at what feels like 5 a.m. after the time change. That can lead to an “early awake pattern,” make it harder to fall asleep the next night, and shift a person’s schedule in a way that can take time to fix. Creighton said it can take a number of days, and sometimes even a couple of weeks, to fully adjust.
 Why the disruption matters comes down to how sleep works. Creighton said the body has two main systems that drive sleep: sleep pressure, which builds the longer you’re awake, and the circadian rhythm, a daily 24-ish hour cycle that helps determine when you feel sleepy and when you feel alert. When those two systems are working together, sleep and daytime alertness are more likely to be at their best.
 To get back on track, Creighton recommended focusing on light, movement and consistency. She said natural, bright light, especially in the morning, is one of the most important tools for setting the circadian rhythm each day. Movement during the day can also help, along with keeping a consistent bedtime and wake time and protecting enough hours of sleep.
 As for the growing trend of “light clocks” designed to wake people up more gently, Creighton said they can help, though she noted they may be “a little bit more gimmicky.” She said sunlight is probably best, and a sun lamp can also be a strong option.
 Some everyday habits can make the adjustment harder. Creighton said caffeine too close to bedtime can disrupt sleep, and suggested a rule of thumb: try to avoid caffeine six to eight hours before bed. She added that some people are more sensitive and may need even more time than that. Screens can also be a problem, not only because of the light, but because of stimulation, “doom scrolling,” and bedtime procrastination that can push bedtime later than it should be. On the flip side, Creighton said exercise during the day can be helpful for sleep.
 If sleep problems continue even after trying those strategies, Creighton said the next step is to talk to a doctor. She said abrupt time changes can sometimes unmask an underlying issue. Anyone who has plenty of opportunity to sleep but still doesn’t feel rested, has trouble sleeping, or has a partner noticing symptoms like snoring or gasping awake should bring it up with their doctor.
 And for parents dealing with little ones who are suddenly wide awake earlier than usual, Creighton said a gradual approach may work better than expecting kids to handle a full one-hour shift overnight. She suggested slowly adjusting wake-up and morning time by about 10 to 15 minutes a day over the course of several weeks, rather than making the full jump all at once.
